claims.text: What the strip looks like Sharp vertical spikes right before the paced complex; modern bipolar pacers make small spikes that can be subtle.
claims.quote: Sharp vertical deflections immediately preceding the paced complex. Modern bipolar pacers produce small spikes that can be subtle.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Pacing spikes: vertical spikes of short duration, usually 2 ms; may be hard to see in every lead
claims.quote: Vertical spikes of short duration, usually 2 ms. May be difficult to see in all leads.

claims.text: Spike size: bipolar leads give much smaller spikes than unipolar leads; epicardial leads give smaller spikes than endocardial leads
claims.quote: Bipolar leads result in a much smaller pacing spike than unipolar leads. Epicardially placed leads result in smaller pacing spikes than endocardially placed leads.

claims.text: Atrial pacing: the spike precedes the P wave; P morphology depends on lead placement but may look normal
claims.quote: Pacing spike precedes the p wave. Morphology of p wave dependent of lead placement but may appear normal.

claims.text: Ventricular pacing: the spike precedes the QRS; an RV lead gives an LBBB-like QRS (a left epicardial lead gives an RBBB-like QRS)
claims.quote: Pacing spike precedes the QRS complex. Right ventricle pacing lead placement results in a QRS morphology similar to LBBB. Left epicardial pacing lead placement results in a QRS morphology similar to RBBB.

claims.text: ST/T (ventricular pacing): should be discordant with the QRS — the ST segment and T wave sit on the opposite side of the baseline from the main terminal part of the QRS
claims.quote: ST segments and T waves should be discordant with the QRS complex i.e. the major terminal portion of the QRS complex is located on the opposite side of the baseline from the ST segment and T wave.

claims.text: Dual-chamber pacing: spikes may precede only the P wave, only the QRS, or both
claims.quote: Pacing spikes may precede only p wave, only QRS complex, or both.

claims.text: No paced complexes: does not always mean pacemaker failure — it may reflect satisfactory native conduction
claims.quote: The absence of paced complexes does not always mean pacemaker failure as it may reflect satisfactory native conduction.

claims.text: PR (atrial pacing): when paced faster than their AV node can handle, patients can show 1st degree AV block or Wenckebach; not clinically important if cardiac output is not compromised
claims.quote: When these patients are paced at a faster rate than their AV node can handle, the AV node becomes "fatigued" resulting in 1st degree AV block or Wenckebach phenomenon on the paced ECG. This abnormality is not clinically important provided that the patient's cardiac output is not compromised.

claims.text: Ischemia in a paced rhythm: use modified Sgarbossa criteria, as with LBBB
claims.quote: Use modified Sgarbossa criteria, as with LBBB.
claims.locator: 13. Pacemakers, Ischemia in a Paced Rhythm

claims.text: Pacing code (NASPE/BPEG) Letters: five; the first three are used most — chamber paced (A, V, D = both, O = none), chamber sensed, response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = both)
claims.quote: Five letters; first three are most used clinically: 1. Chamber paced (A, V, D = both, O = none) 2. Chamber sensed 3. Response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = both)

claims.text: Position IV: rate modulation, to meet physiological needs (e.g., physical activity)
claims.quote: Position IV: Rate Modulation Indicates ability for rate modulation designed to altered heart appropriately to meet physiological needs e.g. physical activity.

claims.text: Position V: multisite pacing — more than one stimulation site within one anatomical area
claims.quote: Position V: Multisite Pacing Allows indication of multiple stimulation sites within one anatomical area

claims.text: AAI: if native atrial activity is sensed, pacing is inhibited; if none is sensed for a set time, the atrium is paced; used in sinus node dysfunction with intact AV conduction
claims.quote: If native atrial activity sensed then pacing is inhibited. If no native activity sensed for pre-determined time then atrial pacing initiated. Used in sinus node dysfunction with intact AV conduction.

claims.text: VVI: ventricular pace, ventricular sense, inhibited by native beats
claims.quote: VVI: Ventricular pace, ventricular sense, inhibited by native beats

claims.text: VVI is used in chronic atrial impairment (e.g., atrial fibrillation or flutter)
claims.quote: Used in patients with chronic atrial impairment e.g. atrial fibrillation or flutter.

claims.text: DDD: dual-chamber pace and sense with both inhibition and triggering
claims.quote: DDD: Dual-chamber pace and sense with both inhibition and triggering

claims.text: DDD is the commonest pacing mode
claims.quote: Commonest pacing mode.

claims.text: Magnet Magnet on a pacemaker: usually switches to an asynchronous mode (AOO, VOO or DOO) that paces at a constant rate regardless of the native rhythm; the exact mode varies with set-up and manufacturer
claims.quote: This mode varies with pacemaker set-up and manufacturer. Usually initiates an asynchronous pacing mode – AOO, VOO, or DOO. Asynchronous modes deliver constant rate paced stimuli regardless of native rate of rhythm.

claims.text: Asynchronous ventricular pacing carries a risk of pacemaker-induced VT
claims.quote: In asynchronous ventricle pacing there is a risk of pacemaker-induced ventricular tachycardia.

claims.text: Magnet on an ICD: deactivates the defibrillator instead
claims.quote: Note this differs from magnet application to an Implantable Cardioversion Defibrillator (ICD) which results in defibrillator deactivation.
